job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Sara Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at half eight at a logistics company near the port in Valencia, where I'm on a graduate scheme in procurement. I compare quotes from trucking and warehouse suppliers, negotiate small contract changes and keep a tracker of what we pay. I use an AI assistant every day to draft emails to suppliers and to clean up messy price lists, and I eat lunch on the terrace with two other graduates, Irene and Mateo.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a business degree with a good result and spent a summer in the purchasing department of a food factory, which I liked more than I expected. I'm renting a room with my boyfriend Pablo, who's a physiotherapist. My parents are both teachers and can help me in an emergency, but I still owe about 12 thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's useful and that's fine, but it won't change much. I'd tell Irene and Mateo that we should stay sharp on negotiation, because that's what clients pay for. Online I'd say people oversell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the tools are good enough for my job already, so a plateau just means I keep the same edge. My worry is money. Rent in Valencia is up, I owe 12 thousand, and the logistics business runs on thin margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my way up to a buyer role in two years, which pays about a quarter more. I'd save 250 a month and keep paying the loan slowly. I'd also take an evening course in supply-chain data, since it makes my CV more interesting anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small knot about money. It's the kind of world where I plan and don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned thin margins. What would happen if the company struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The graduate scheme is the first place they'd save, I think. I'd be offered a smaller role or let go. I'd start looking at other logistics firms and the port authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Pablo split costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We pay rent in half and he covers more of the food. If one of us lost income, the other would carry the rent for a few months, but it would be tight for both of us.

say: I'd say it's **useful**, but it won't change much.
I'd tell colleagues to stay sharp on **negotiation**, because that's what clients pay for.
think: The tools already suit my job, so a plateau means I keep my **edge**.
My real worry is **money**: rent is up, I owe 12 thousand and margins are thin.
do: Work towards a **buyer** role in two years, with about a quarter more pay.
Save **250 a month** and pay the loan slowly.
Take an evening course in **supply-chain data**.
feel: Mostly fine, with a small **knot** about money.
S0.quote: The graduate scheme is the first place they'd save, I think.
fieldNote: Sara's unease is about **rent and thin margins**, not AI.
She treats her AI use as normal, which is typical of an adaptive profile.
Her shared costs with boyfriend Pablo give a small buffer.

steps.text: Keep comparing supplier quotes and aim for the buyer role in two years
Save 250 a month while paying the loan slowly
Take the evening supply-chain data course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should use it on purpose, not by accident. I'd propose that our team write down which parts of procurement the tool does well, such as comparing quotes, and which need a person, like negotiating when a supplier is late. Online I'd share what I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the routine half of my job, the comparing and the drafting, will go to software in a few years. The negotiating and relationships will last longer. Graduate schemes might shrink, because the firm needs fewer people to do the junior work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools for even more of the grunt work and spend the freed hours on supplier visits and negotiation. I'd also ask my manager, Elena, about moving into category management. And I'd start building a small portfolio of savings cases, to show what I've saved the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think I'm in a better spot than most, but I'm not the only one with this idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're in a better spot than most. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm already fast with the tools and I like the people side. A lot of my classmates avoided the tools or did a purely number-based job. I think it will separate people quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the graduate scheme was cut next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a smaller company where I'd do more of everything, or I'd try the port authority. I'd also probably say yes to a job in another city, because Pablo can work almost anywhere.

I'd suggest the team write down what the tool does **well** and what needs a person.

The **negotiating** and relationships will last longer, but graduate schemes may shrink.

Keep a portfolio of **savings cases** I've delivered.
feel: **Uneasy**, but I think I'm in a better spot than most.
S1.quote: I'm already fast with the tools and I like the people side.
fieldNote: Sara sees AI as a **sorting force** among graduates and thinks she is on the right side.
Her portfolio of savings cases is a concrete way to prove value.
Pablo's flexible job gives her mobility.

steps.text: Use the assistant for price-list cleaning and supplier emails each day
Ask Elena about moving into category management
Build a spreadsheet tool that tracks savings and flags late suppliers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask the managers what the plan is for the graduate scheme and every other role. Online I'd read a lot and share what's sensible. I'd also tell Pablo and my parents on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the comparing and drafting go in months, and the negotiation work follows soon after. I'm adaptive, but two years is a very short time for anyone. I'd be fighting for a handful of roles that still need a human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as hard as I can, about 600 a month, and cut anything extra. I'd look for roles where a person still has to be in the room, like port operations or supplier relations in a physical warehouse. I'd also consider a move abroad if the jobs were elsewhere, and I'd apply for a few retraining places on a data course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel the clock more than anything, like an exam when you haven't revised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned roles where a person has to be in the room. Is that a good bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about three years, yes, because robots for hands-on work come later. After that, I'm not sure. A hands-on job is a bridge, not a destination.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, don't worry, I have a plan, even if I don't, because Mum would otherwise call every day. Then on the weekend I'd tell them the truth, that I'm scared but moving.

say: I'd ask managers what the **plan** is for the graduate scheme.
I'd tell Pablo and my **parents** on day one.
think: The comparing and drafting go in **months**, and negotiation follows soon after.
Two years is very short, so I'd fight for a few roles that need a **human**.
do: Save about **600 a month** and cut extras.
Look for roles where a **person** has to be in the room, like port operations.

feel: **Anxious**, with the clock more than anything, like an exam without revision.
S2.quote: A hands-on job is a bridge, not a destination.
fieldNote: Sara has a plan but is honest that the **hands-on bridge** lasts only three years.
She would tell her parents a comforting line first, then the truth.
Willing to move abroad, showing adaptive flexibility.

steps.text: Save about 600 a month and cut subscriptions and meals out
Cancel the gym and weekend trips for a year
Apply for port operations and supplier relations jobs
Apply for data and logistics jobs in other countries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years gives us time to redesign roles, and I'd suggest we start now. Online I'd probably share what I learn about careers that stay human-facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but hopeful. In five years I'd be 27, with a track record and a good network. If I stay ahead with the tools, I can probably find a role that matters, but I'd keep a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a category manager, then add a part-time master's in supply chain analytics, which my firm might help pay for. I'd save 400 a month and put a little into an index fund. And I'd keep my network warm, because jobs come through people more than adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than scared. It feels like a long hike with a cliff at the end, and I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep a plan B. What is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something with Pablo, like opening a small practice management service for physios, using my business skills. It's a little crazy, but it's the sort of thing that's possible when tools make things cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you do compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'm in survival mode. With five years I can study and move up one level before the change, so I arrive as someone with a title, not as a graduate.

I'd share what I learn about careers that stay **human-facing**.
think: I'd be uneasy but hopeful, **27** with a track record and a network.

Save **400 a month** and put a little in an index fund.

feel: **Uneasy**, more than scared, like a long hike with a cliff at the end.
S3.quote: With five years I can study and move up one level before the change, so I arrive as someone with a title, not as a graduate.
fieldNote: Sara's plan is **to climb a level** before the change arrives.
Her plan B is a small service business with her boyfriend Pablo.
Adaptive style shows in the willingness to build the business.

steps.text: Move up to category manager within two years
Start a part-time master's in supply chain analytics
Save 400 a month for a safety cushion
Put 100 a month into an index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to redesign things properly. At work I'd mentor the next graduates, and online I'd write about what I learn. I'd stay curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a decade of using the tools and a few contacts across the industry. I'd probably be in management or running a small business, and I'd have options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd climb to category manager, then head of procurement at a mid-size firm if I could. I'd save 300 a month, buy a flat with Pablo and put money in an index fund. I'd also pick a field where a human voice still matters, like negotiation or relationship management, and get good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit curious. It's the one where I'm excited to see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the tools get so good, so quickly, that being good at them stops being special. Everyone's going to be fast, and then it's about judgement and trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone just starting a business degree in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools in your first year, learn how to talk to people by your second, and pick something a person still has to do. And don't plan for one world, plan for a few.

say: I'd say ten years is a **real chance** to redesign things properly.
At work I'd **mentor** the next graduates.
think: I'd feel good, since by 2036 I'd be **32** with a decade of tool use.
I'd probably be in **management** or running a small business, with options.
do: Climb to **category manager**, then head of procurement.
Save **300 a month** and buy a flat with Pablo.
Get good at **negotiation** and relationship management.
feel: **Calm** and curious, excited to see what happens.
S4.quote: Everyone's going to be fast, and then it's about judgement and trust.
fieldNote: Sara's calm rests on **time and skills**, not on security of the sector.

Advice to new students is practical and her own.

steps.text: Climb to category manager and then head of procurement
Save 300 a month towards a flat deposit
Put part of the savings into an index fund each month
Buy a flat with Pablo when the deposit is ready

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because even I can't build a new career in two years while the old one disappears. What would help is a steady retraining income and employers who say honestly which roles stay. Also, a place to compare notes with people in the same boat would help me think.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I rely on the tools already. If I was told tomorrow to work without the tools, I'd be slower than my parents were at my age. I'm not sure whether that is a skill or a weakness.

headlineQuote: If I was told tomorrow to work without the tools, I'd be slower than my parents were at my age.
portrait: Sara, 22, is on a **procurement graduate scheme** at a logistics company near Valencia's port.
She uses an **AI assistant** every day and rents a room with her boyfriend Pablo, owing about 12 thousand.
Centre and adaptive, she tries to **climb a level** before each change arrives.
Her mood moves from uneasy to **anxious** at two years, then to calm when there are ten years.
Teacher parents are her emergency cushion, and she'd move abroad if the jobs were elsewhere.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because even she cannot build a new career in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A steady **retraining income** and employers who say honestly which roles stay.
